utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Please be seated. The case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Radakovic. You are prepared to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, please, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, could you tell us what the procedure was in Prijedor in 1992 where you worked, and in the period of 1996 through 1997, when you wanted to take time off or request sick leave.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went on sick leave. Therefore, I don't know what the procedure was. In 1997, mostly there were neither sick leaves nor annual leaves. I didn't take my annual leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In order to have a record of the time that you had worked, did someone have to sign a record that you had worked those hours?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The hours were not accounted. But when somebody was away for the day, that would enter the record, as well as when that person was in. That also went into the record. There was a special service which counted the days when people worked as opposed to the days when they didn't work. There was a special service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic sign your time records?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dr. Stakic didn't sign, and very often it would happen to me that I would be absent for an hour. I didn't have to ask Dr. Stakic's permission but my superior in my service, who was my head of service. He was my superior, I took orders from him, and he was the one who signed all the documents, for example, decisions on annual leaves, that we didn't take, and decisions on my salary. So I would go to that service, and I would tell them I have to take my mother to the doctor's. I never went to see a doctor myself. And then there would be a replacement, somebody who would replace me for an hour or two hours during the time while I was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was it a common practice in your workplace that on occasions such as someone's birthday, such as a wedding, or on sadder occasions such as the death of a family member, that a card would be circulated in the office, to have the colleagues sign that card?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no cards. If you had to express your condolences, you didn't do it in writing. And since you've mentioned somebody's death, my father died in January 1996. That's when I was absent. And I believe that I was absent for one whole working week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did Dr. Stakic send you any letter or communication with his condolences?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, how do you know Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Simo Drljaca from before the war. He lived above my parents while he worked as a lawyer in the education fund. I don't know what the name of the institution was, but anyway, it was an organisation in charge of primary education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you socialise with him? Did you know him well?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were just sort of nodding acquaintances so to say. We just would nod and greet each other passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On page 69 of yesterday's transcript - and I'm quoting the page number, madam, just so you know, so the Judge and Mr. Lukic can follow along - beginning on line 1, you indicated that you went "to see Mr. Drljaca and asked him for a favour, and the favour was for my son not to be sent to the war." Why was it that you asked Mr. Drljaca to keep your son from being sent to the war?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at the time, my son was a member of the reserve police. He left at the beginning of June and he ended up with the police at the end of September. On the 1st of October, 1992, he reported to his occupational specialty unit, and he had some objections about being sent to Orasje or something like that. And that was at the time when the police was getting ready to go to Orasje. That is when I paid a visit to Simo Drljaca. Until that moment, I didn't know him very well. And from then onwards, we hardly even said hello to each other. When I was in his office, I told him, "If your Sinisa was on the list --" that is his son's name, Sinisa -- "and if I was the one who had to sign the list, then your Sinisa, your son would not be sent to the front line, I assure you."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was your son's name Rade?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What is your son's name?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did he have the nickname "Srbo"?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, his nickname is "Misko."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You said your son was in the reserve police. Was it a particular unit of the reserve police that your son was in?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the beginning when they kept guard at checkpoints in town. That's why I told him to join them, because if nothing else, at least he could spend nights at home, not on the front line. It may sound selfish to you, but I am a mother and only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was your son a member of the Intervention Platoon?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you have heard of this -- have you heard of the Intervention Platoon?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, you indicated that the Crisis Staff meetings were in the basement, in the communications room. Is my memory correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a proper conference room. Those were the rooms from which alerts were given to the population. That was a special unit that alerted the population, and it was a department before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In addition to that room, did they meet in the large conference room?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know when they held meetings. Downstairs, I didn't know when they held meetings. Upstairs, if it was during the working hours, I didn't see it, so I wasn't aware of when and where they held their meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, did you ever call, on behalf of Dr. Stakic, Mr. Budimir, Slavko Budimir?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, although it is possible. But I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you call to come to meetings Ranko Travar for Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were not meetings, they were just briefings. He was the head of finance department, and it was a very important secretariat for everyday life. Everything relies and begins with finances; the supply of town with petrol, food, electricity, and other necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you call, on behalf of Dr. Stakic, Mr. Vojo Pavicic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are people who were heads of particular bodies or organs, and they would meet at sessions of the Executive Board. And I believe that Vojo Pavicic was among those who came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. But my question is, did you call Vojo Pavicic on behalf of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How about Dr. Zeljko Macura? Did you call him on behalf of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I called Macura. He did not belong to any administrative body, and I don't know what he did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How about Mr. Bosko Mandic? Did you call him on behalf of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosko Mandic joined the Executive Board when Stakic was no longer there. That's, at least, what I believe; while Dr. Kovacevic was there, or something like that, or with Dr. Kovacevic. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall making calls to Mr. Bosko Mandic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You've mentioned the name of Dr. Kovacevic. How often would Dr. Kovacevic come to Dr. Stakic's office in 1992 after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hard for me to say or give you a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, was it something that would happen on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no regular intervals at which they would meet. Dr. Stakic would sometimes go there even if he was not invited -- sorry, this was a slip of the tongue. Dr. Kovacevic, I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How far away was the office of Dr. Kovacevic from the office of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two large rooms between their two offices. I don't know how much would that be in metres, maybe 30 metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. They were on the same floor, just so -- just to make that clear. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could have the witness shown the diagram D49.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, from Dr. Stakic's office -- and now I'm talking not about the office he sat in as vice-president of the Municipal Assembly but the office that he sat in after the takeover, are there windows in that office?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which office? All the offices have windows. There's no single office in the municipal building without a window, or at least, I don't know of any such office without a window.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The windows in Dr. Stakic's office, can you tell us what they looked out on? Did they look towards the museum? Can you tell us, what would you see when you looked out of those windows? And you can explain if they were on just one side or two sides of the office there were windows, please.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the building, and approximately --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you mean. Okay. This is the entrance to the building. My office is approximately at the middle of this gallery. This is a gallery or a balcony. This is the president's office, and then a small room, and then the Executive Board towards the end of the building. From this -- you've mentioned the museum. The museum, as far as I can tell on this map, this could be the museum. Not directly, but from an angle you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've made that clear. Can you show us -- before we leave this diagram, where is the large meeting room? Was there a large meeting room in the Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is this large meeting room, on the second floor above us. And its windows look on both sides, on this side and on that side, even on this side. There are also glass sort of windows or doors, but you can't open those doors or windows. So actually, there are glass windows on three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm just going to try to describe for the record so that someone reading can understand what you've pointed to. When we're talking about Dr. Stakic's office, you pointed towards the centre of the building, near the entrance, just -- on the diagram, just to the right of the entrance. When you talked -- and that was the office of the president. When we talked about the Municipal Assembly meeting room, the large meeting room, you pointed to the top of the building, or the left top of the building, that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Counsel and the Court agree or correct me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be also helpful to add that it was at the side heading towards, in part, museum, and from a different angle, also in the direction to the MUP or SUP building. So in front -- in any event, in front of the building at the same side where the main entrance was. Correct? Were the windows at the side where the main entrance is shown on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The big conference room -- I'm afraid I didn't understand your question well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... about the office of Dr. Stakic in the period after April 30th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates] [Interpretation] I don't know. What am I expected to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be at the side of the building where we can also see the main entrance. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, you talked about -- you said that Dr. Stakic did not call Mr. Drljaca. Did you ever receive calls from Mr. Drljaca for Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see in Dr. Stakic's office members of the Prijedor press?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- you mean during the war, the period after April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Let's say after the takeover of the municipality on the 30th of April until Dr. Stakic left in 1993 his position, did you see members of the press from Prijedor in Dr. Stakic's office?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a meeting, but it was held - and I believe that we spoke about that yesterday - when members of the press came, and I don't know which month that was. I believe it was the end of July, or maybe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Just so I understand, I believe now you're talking about the time that foreign journalists came to Prijedor and went to the camps.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before that, did you ever see, for example, Zivko Ecim? Did he come to Dr. Stakic's office?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember -- first, do you know Rade Mutic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him. He is also a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did he phone, did he call, or did he come to the office of Dr. Stakic, or did Dr. Stakic place calls to Mr. Mutic in 1992 after the takeover, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Aprilski - forgive me if I'm mispronouncing the name - did you know him; one of the editors of Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Aprilski, I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You talked about the day of the takeover and coming to work. And you said that you didn't notice any changes. Let me go -- excuse me, for counsel, page 61, line 10 of yesterday's LiveNote, beginning on line 9. You told Mr. Ostojic: "I went to the Municipal Assembly building. I went to work as usual. There were no apparent changes, however standing at the door of the Municipal Assembly I saw two young men in uniform." After the takeover, there was sandbags built up in front of the entrance to the Municipal Assembly building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular detail. We used to refer to those as barricades, but I believe that was only following the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During the time that you worked with Dr. Stakic after the takeover in 1992, do you recall him ever complaining about the work of any other persons in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not to me. We didn't discuss such things, such things as him being unhappy about someone else's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic ever complain in your presence about the accuracy or the work of the Official Gazette or of press articles?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would Dr. Stakic receive reports, to your knowledge, of interrogations that took place at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I asked you a question yesterday that perhaps was not as clear as it should have been about whether you kept Dr. Stakic's agenda, and I want to make sure that there's not a problem in the word I'm using. What I mean to ask you is did you keep Dr. Stakic's schedule of meetings, in other words, his appointments? Would you keep a record that at 11.00 on Thursday, Mr. Travar wants to come to see Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. If there had been such a meeting, the two of them would have been in direct contact, and then they would come and visit each other, especially in the afternoon when I didn't...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, how many times, to your knowledge -- how often would the Crisis Staff meet? And I'm referring to the Crisis Staff in Prijedor after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not convene the Crisis Staff, so I can't say how often. I'm not sure. And then I'm better off not saying anything. Whether it was once a day, once a week, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, wasn't it part of your responsibilities to know where Dr. Stakic was so that if someone came to see him or called him, you would be able to say, "He's in a meeting in the basement," for example, "and will be back in an hour, expected back"?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were moments when Dr. Stakic would just go and say, "I'm going to a meeting." Now, where the meeting was taking place, I really don't know. The Executive Board, perhaps, or the Crisis Staff, as you say. Whether it was in the basement or in a different place, I really don't know. It may have been in the big hall also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, if there was an urgent reason to contact Dr. Stakic, wasn't it important for you to know where he was?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Then I asked the other people in the service who else went to the meeting - I could have known approximately - but no one said where they were, what the meeting was or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So do I take it from your answer that you don't know how often the Crisis Staff met? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic convene, to your knowledge, meetings of the National Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Dr. Stakic didn't. The Secretariat for National Defence was in charge of that, people who worked for them, whoever was in charge of that particular thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, aren't you aware that the chairman of the National Defence Council for Prijedor or the president was, by law, the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. We say "by virtue of his office," the president of the council was always the president of the municipality, both in peacetime and in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this was a body that brought together the police, the military, and the civilian leadership of the municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was there in that body during the war, or who was present, because I wasn't the one convening the meetings. I think not the civilian authorities or the army, but before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So your testimony is that before the war, the civilians, the army -- correct me if I'm wrong, the way I understand your answer, that the civilians, the police, and the army would meet and confer, but not during the war.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is that I didn't know about during the war because I didn't convene these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You talked about an argument you overheard between Dr. Stakic, or hearing them, Dr. Stakic and Mr. Drljaca arguing. Did you hear what they argued about?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But they were very loud. I said I had to stand up and close the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So all you know was that they were speaking in very loud voices.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they really raised their voice. I could almost say they were swearing at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, when Dr. Stakic came back to power in Prijedor, you indicated you thought it was 1996, who became the chief of police of Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. If you remind me, perhaps then I'll know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, Simo Drljaca came back and served as the chief of police, with Dr. Stakic as the president of the Municipal Assembly, up until the time he was killed following his attempted arrest in July 1997. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you attend the funeral of Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I had my own reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Can we go to a closed session, as we did yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And to be redacted from the video and... Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps it might be useful for me to restate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, after the takeover, from the 30th of April, 1992, through the end of September, you were aware that massive crimes were occurring in Prijedor against citizens of Croat and Muslim ethnicity. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Massive crimes, I don't know about massive crimes. I think that may be a bit too harsh. But later, in September or thereabouts, I did learn about some things like that. And again, I didn't hear this in the office where I worked, I heard it from my neighbours and people talking. None of this was ever said in any of the offices where I worked. People didn't talk about that. I had a serious relationship with Dr. Stakic, and not only with Dr. Stakic but rather with all the presidents that I worked for. They didn't talk to me about what they discussed at any of their meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm now talking about what you saw and knew in 1992. You told us that you knew that a mosque in the town, the main mosque, was destroyed and burned in July of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 11th of July, just before St. Peter's day. I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In fact, all of the mosques, all of the churches in Prijedor were destroyed in 1992, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the mosque in Puharska, too. It was destroyed. The young man I mentioned yesterday, he lived nearby. He told us that. My son's friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There was a --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzko, we used to call him Nedzko. I didn't see that myself because I couldn't see it. It was too far for me to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Lukic, do there need to be any redactions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, I just wanted to make sure it was okay to mention the name of your son's friend. In fact, you knew that your son's friend was in the Omarska camp, so you knew that there was a camp where people were held under horrible conditions. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the circumstances, because I wasn't there. But when my son received a message from this friend of his, it was written on a slip of paper used to wrap biscuits in. Then my reaction was as I described yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In fact, you were so concerned with the survival of that young man that you swallowed your pride and went to speak to your ex-husband about that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Because you knew that that was a camp where horrible things were being done to people. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back then, I didn't know, but later, yes, I did hear that. This young man didn't tell me anything, and he never said that anyone had done anything to him or that he had been physically abused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Living in Prijedor, you had seen that Stari Grad had been completely destroyed, both of its mosques and all of the houses except for one or two were destroyed and eventually bulldozed. You saw Kozarac and the Brdo area had been destroyed. Houses burned. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I only went back to the old town after the war, because I simply couldn't go there. I only saw Kozarac after the war also, because there was no need for me, during the war, to go in the direction of Banja Luka. We didn't drive around in our cars exactly because we were short of petrol. Petrol was a very rare and precious commodity. Throughout the whole war, I never once entered my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, for a year and a half, you worked with Muhamed Cehajic. And correct me if I am wrong, but you had a good relationship with him, and you saw him as a very -- a man of integrity who treated all people very well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You knew, in 1992, that he had been arrested and disappeared from the Omarska camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know until much later, two or three months later. People just didn't talk about these things. At least, I was never told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you know of any Muslim or Croat that Dr. Stakic helped or tried to help in Prijedor after the takeover of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know. Stakic never spoke to me about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know of anything that Dr. Stakic did or tried to do to stop crimes from happening in Prijedor against the citizens of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I'm not a politician myself. No one told me anything about these things, nor was I in any position to see for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe I do not have any further questions at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did think of one. I don't know if you want me to do it now. I did think of one area I forgot to cover. I could probably do it in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, what do you know about why Dr. Stakic left the position of president of the municipality at the end of 1992, early 1993?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me officially why, but I heard that there had been disagreements within the party and that that was why he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, in 1997, you said you came back from a sick leave and Dr. Stakic was no longer coming to work. Did you have any contact with him after that time?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I was on sick leave in 1997. That was in 1996, in January, between the 23rd of January and -- you've got me confused now. I can't even remember on which day my father died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me just then go to -- do you recall the day that Mr. Kovacevic was arrested and Mr. Drljaca was killed?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you working --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at work in those days. I was on sick leave for two months. I was getting my teeth fixed. And I had a visitor, and that's why I remember clearly that I was not at work during those months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you testified on page 80, you were asked: "When you came back to work, was Dr. Stakic still coming to work as the president of the Municipal Assembly?" Line 13. And you answered, "No." Is that correct? When you came back from having your teeth fixed, Dr. Stakic was no longer coming to work. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have any contact with him? Did he ever call you? Did you ever see him after Dr. Kovacevic was arrested? Let's just use that as the point.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did he in any way communicate to you, or did you see any communication by him as to why he stopped coming to work? Did you see it in the media? Did you see it in the Municipal Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were rumours, but I don't know precisely what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The rumours were that he had left Prijedor because of Dr. Kovacevic's arrest. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I know is that he went to pursue further studies. That's what I learned later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say learned that later on, when did you learn that? Was that this week you learned that?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps two or three months after the date you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam, I have sometimes difficulties with my sense of orientation. And we are grateful that you described on the map where the office of Dr. Stakic was located. It was on the first or on the second floor of the building?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first floor. You have the ground floor, the first floor, the second floor, and that's all. His was on the first floor, in the middle of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to present to the witness this piece of paper and put it on the ELMO and give at the same time a pencil or a pen to her. May this document be provisionally marked as J26. You can see my more or less helpless attempt to draw a sketch on the first floor. And to the left-hand side, I wanted to indicate that's the area where the entrance was. Could you please assist us and show us where and from which side the staircase arrived at the first floor.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I use the pen to draw? This middle part, is that supposed to be the corridor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My attempt was the line in the middle, this should be the corridor. Maybe I'm totally wrong and it was not such a corridor, but then, please assist me.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just turn the paper this way to start with.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the staircases leading from the first floor upstairs, and all of this is the hallway or the corridor. These are the offices. And this here, these are also offices. This is the hallway, but the entrance is on the other side. Not here but on the other side. And the staircase is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. And can you then please indicate on this sketch where was your office.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here. "M," my.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would mean that your office had no window heading to the side where the entrance was. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large window -- there was a balcony, and I could open the door to the balcony. I could come out to the balcony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But heading to the back side of the building. Do you regard the part of the building where the entrance was the front side?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, the entrance was here. All the windows are here. This is the municipal building. There are windows on the side as well, but those were the windows of the offices looking at the other side. And our offices were on the front of the building. It was the southern side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I apologise when my -- as I already previously said, unhelpful attempt to draw a sketch about the real entrance. On the map, we saw an entrance. So this would mean that the entrance was immediately beyond your office and the balcony of your office. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I may have been wrong. I should have turned the paper the other way around and I would have used your entrance as the real entrance but I may have made a mistake by turning it the way I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We shouldn't discuss mistakes --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on how you look at this piece of paper. I could have drawn everything the other way around, on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so and indicate with your own words where the main entrance of the building was located.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not here. Let's say this is the back side of the building, but here, below this balcony, here is the staircase below. It's protruding a bit further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then we know where we have each other. Could you then indicate the room of Professor Cehajic before the takeover.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And Dr. Stakic's room before the takeover.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my left was the vice-president, and to my right was the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, at that time, in 1992, do you know about other persons having their office on the same corridor? Maybe to be absolutely exact, if there was a change, please indicate. Maybe a person was in an office before April 30th or after. Who else had offices on this corridor?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the offices of communal professional affairs. This is a small conference room, and this is the office of the vice-president of the Executive Board. Am I doing something wrong, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, it just will be extremely difficult to follow this without having it on the transcript. So the office beside the office of Professor Cehajic, this was a conference room. Then it was followed by the office of the vice-president of the Executive Board. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the entrance was from the Executive Board. That's what I'm trying to draw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So once again, the same system; secretary in the middle room, vice-president to one side --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- and president to the other side.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Anybody else you would identify where an office was located?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, it was the way I've drawn it. Maybe you would be interested to know that the employees of the Executive Board were sitting in the offices here, across the corridor. Maybe you would also like to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So just on the other side of the corridor, opposed to the office of the president and the vice-president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we now turn to the other side of the first floor. Who had offices there?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the offices of the technical services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the left-hand side, offices of technical service. This means the office headed by Mr. Dusan Baltic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the secretary of the assembly, Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the remaining offices, please.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this line of offices here, there are only four offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then on the other side, beside the office of Dr. Stakic, these offices were occupied by whom, please?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These offices housed people from the so-called common affairs; the personnel, education. The period of time that I'm talking about is recently, as far as I can remember. I believe that it was so at that time, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This already helped a lot. If you could, please, add, if you know, the names of the vice-president and the president of the Executive Board on this sketch as well.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before the takeover. 1992, January until April.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the Executive Board, Dr. Kovacevic; Vice-president Enes, and I can't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be Kovacevic's room, the first one on the right-hand side; and Enes, you said, the third one on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if the entrance is here, then Kovacevic is on the left, and Enes is on the right. And the situation is the same as it is with my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to ask you this question: Whenever a person wanted to enter the office of Dr. Stakic or the late Professor Cehajic, he had first to go through your office, or were there separate doors to these two offices?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The small conference room here was adjacent to the president's office. From the president's office, one could go to the small conference room, and the small conference room also had a door directly to the corridor. There is also a door from the president's office and from the vice-president's office, but these doors are not really doors. They served as a cupboard, and they were padded. And they never opened. One couldn't open them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in conclusion, whenever a visitor entered one of these two offices, he would have to go through your office. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but also no. If there was a meeting, then I would be told to open the door to the small conference room. Then that conference room would be open, the door would be left open. So if somebody was coming to the meeting, they could do it through the -- directly to the small conference room. Or if somebody wanted to go to the toilet, or if the person who brought coffees and refreshments, they could also enter the small conference room directly. So the meeting would start, would go on, and would finish without me knowing who attended it, who left early or who came later. Given the way the staircase is, it's easier for them to actually go directly from the staircase to the small conference room, rather than come all the way to my office, and then go through three rooms in order to get to the conference room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It becomes clearer and clearer. But I understand it was for you first to open this conference room, the small conference room. Normally, it was closed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often. We kept them closed and locked so nobody would be able to come to the president's office from, so to say, from the back door. So that was the system that we used. So the technical part of my job was always the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand. And from your testimony, I took it that it was a different job to do the work of a typist. The typists were in which floor of the building?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every service or department had either one or two typists. So there were typists everywhere. And the number of typists depended on the size of a particular department or secretariat, as they used to be called. There were no designated offices for typists.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I really have to say that? Because the ladies who worked there, I don't know whether they will appreciate their names being mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand. Let us go in closed session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. I just had forgotten one final point. You mentioned yesterday, and once again today during the cross-examination by Mr. Koumjian, that on the occasion of a dispute, you had to close windows. These were windows in your office, being between the two other offices, or in the room occupied at that time by Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Koumjian, you mean the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And now, excuse me, can you please just try to explain your question about the windows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us that once upon a time, there was a such a loud dispute that you thought it would be better to close the window, that others outside couldn't follow this dispute. These were the windows of your office or the office of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My window, my window. Outside, you couldn't hear, because this was on the first floor. I was the only one who could hear, or anyone else who happened to be sitting with me in the same office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the dispute, I understand, was in your own office at that time?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. In Mr. Stakic's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not that I misunderstand anything, you were in your own office, you heard a dispute in Dr. Stakic's office, and then you entered, proprio motu, the office of Dr. Stakic, and then you closed the window --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I stood up and closed my own window. May I continue, please? I stood up, I closed my own window, which was behind my back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe I have some difficulties today. But when closing your windows, it appears that you heard the dispute or the voices from the open windows of Dr. Stakic's office. And in order not to follow this dispute, you closed your windows because the voice did not come through the wall or the door, but through both windows? Or was there an additional window maybe between your office and the office of the president of the Municipal Assembly? May I ask the usher, please, once again to present Document J26 to the witness. Sorry that I don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So could you please indicate where was the window you closed at that time.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my office. This is the balcony door, and the balcony door also has a window. That's here. The balcony is just outside the president's and vice-president's office. And it has both a balcony door and a window, but the office is twice as big and has another window right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And now, please, once again, cross-mark the window you closed.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This window here. This is the window looking out onto the balcony. And the window is just one part of it. This is the window and the balcony door, a double door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But still I don't know how could this -- closing this window prevent others from listening to the dispute when --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The others, in the sense of someone walking into my office in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. I think I've got the gist of it now. And this concludes the reference to this document. Thank you. This can be removed from the ELMO. Before turning to other questions, I want to proceed based on yesterday's transcript. On page 52, line 13 through 19, you explained your duties as a technical secretary. You received visitors, you talked to the visitors, you answered their telephones, and you would connect calls. That, obviously, depended on whether they wanted to talk to the person who wanted to talk to them. In part, it was already covered by the question by the Prosecution this morning: You received visitors. Did they come by chance and you were not prepared at all to receive those visitors, or did you have a kind of calendar where you made your own notes that a visitor would come because there was an appointment?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that they came, clients would come, business people. I didn't take any notes. Perhaps a name or two, so I could read it out as I was speaking, but it wasn't the sort of paper or notes that I would keep, because I didn't think that I would need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry that we have we go in that details, but related to phone calls, you told us, "I would connect them if they had a call and that also obviously depended on whether they wanted to talk to the person who wanted to talk to them." So a visitor arrived. You had no marks in any calendar. Would you first contact Dr. Stakic or, previously, Professor Cehajic whether or not they wanted to receive this person, they wanted to greet or meet them, or they had no time at all?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When a client walked in -- this is how it looked roughly. A client walks in and says, "I would like to speak to the president or the vice-president." Very often, I would ask about the reason. And then the client would either give me the reason or decline to do so. In that case, I would phone the president or the vice-president if they could see this particular client. If the president was busy, in that case, I would come out and tell the client that the president was unavailable and tell them to come another day. And then the day I told them to come back, the client would remember it, but I didn't keep any records of that because the client would just simply be back, and then I would remember that that was that and that the president would be available on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the case at that point in time the president was absent, and the client would ask, "What would be the appropriate point in time that in all likelihood I would and could meet Dr. Stakic?" what would be your answer?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that moment, I would tell the client that I would tell the president about that, and then that the client could come back at a different time to see what the response would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you mentioned beforehand, it is your testimony that you had no overview at all on the availability in the office of, be it the president or the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There weren't such big meetings that you couldn't remember back in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apart big meetings, to the best of your recollection, do you know for what purposes this conference room close to the office of Dr. Stakic at that time, for which purposes this conference room was used? Who met there?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That office was used normally if the president had one client in his office, and there was another client he was supposed to be seeing. In that case, he would go to this small hall - that's how we referred to this hall - he would open the door and see this other client if the matter was urgent. As far as meetings, obviously when things got going, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn now to another topic. On page 56, lines 2 through 6 on LiveNote, you were asked: "Could in 1991 and 1992 the president of the Municipal Assembly fire, discharge, or dismiss you from your employment that you held?" And your answer was: "No. That would take a major violation, and then there would be a disciplinary committee which would decide." Given the case, you wouldn't report for a period of five days or more to work, would this be a major violation, allowing for dismissal?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would depend on the reason why you were absent. It's up to your direct superior to decide on that, not the president of the municipality. My superior, my absence could have been justified. I could have been sick without even reporting. But if after five days I appeared with a medical explanation, with a medical justification, then obviously that would have been accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And in case there wouldn't be such a -- forget about now your person as such, but in principle, if there wasn't such apology or justifying your absence from work or another person's absence from work, would it then be as you quoted yesterday, for a disciplinary committee to decide whether a dismissal is justified or not?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the book of regulations governing our employment, it says that if you fail to report for three or five or six, or I don't know exactly how many days, entails a certain responsibility, of which nature exactly, I don't know. But during my time at work, not a single person was dismissed simply because they failed to show up for work for five consecutive days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you know about the existence of such a disciplinary committee?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? Now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In 1992 and, more precise, two-fold, before the takeover and after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I do know that before the party arrivals, the president and the vice-president, when the parties came to power, until then, yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was the purpose of my question, because in fact you were answered whether in 1991 and 1992, there could be a dismissal on this or that basis, and then it was for you to answer covering two years; but now I wanted to concentrate the question on the period from January 1992 through April 1992, and then the next period following the takeover. And you yourself mentioned that there would be a disciplinary committee which would decide. Once again, was there, before the takeover and after the takeover, such a disciplinary committee?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was the reason, may I ask, that yesterday you said, "Then there would be a disciplinary committee which would decide"?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I haven't understood the question, that it's only referring to a certain period, or normally, otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On today's transcript, page 39, line 9, you stated: "I didn't know about that. I do know that before the party arrivals, the president and the vice-president, when the parties came to power, until then, yes, there was." There was what, please?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The disciplinary committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Until then, you are sure that there was such a committee; later, you don't know. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, now it was my fault. For the protection of the witness, may the entire question please be redacted from the transcript and I repeat it in closed session. Sorry for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May the public be removed from the public gallery. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it possible to do it private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. It's easier for the public gallery, we do it in private session. Do you agree? Okay. All the parties agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yesterday, transcript page 64, and also today, you mentioned Mr. Cehajic seeking to talk to Dr. Stakic. What about Minka Cehajic? Did she ever try to contact Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was at the beginning of June, but I can't remember exactly. She said she needed to speak to Dr. Stakic, and I put her through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You put her through immediately on the first attempt?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Immediately. The very moment after I had had a word with the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true, ma'am, that Minka Cehajic asked you whether it would be possible, to quote from our transcript, page 2693, line 22, whether it would be possible to come the following day?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that being said. I know I just put her through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true, madam, that the following morning, she arrived at about 9.30 in the office? Same page of the transcript; 2693.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You said, on today's transcript, page 41, line 24, that Minka Cehajic, "I think it was at the beginning of June, but I can't remember exactly." May it be possible that she tried to come in contact with Dr. Stakic already the 3rd or the 4th of May? So several days after the takeover, end of quote, line 25, page 2693.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the takeover, it was Mr. Cehajic who spoke to Dr. Stakic. I don't remember that Minka did the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And it's your testimony, as you sit here, that you never saw Minka Cehajic in either your office or the office of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I saw Minka Cehajic after the war. We bumped into each other. We sat down, had a cup of coffee together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to apologise. I just confused the transcript. The meeting with -- what I just discussed - and my sincere apologies - the questions were related to a meeting with Mr. Muharem Murselovic. Sorry for this. Did he ask immediately after the takeover to get in touch with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murselovic, I don't remember. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, it's the same page of the transcript. Isn't it true that Mr. Murselovic asked you to get in touch with Dr. Stakic and that you told him to come the following day?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You remember that the following morning, he, in fact, arrived at about 9.30?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that Murselovic mentioned that in a conversation, but I can't really remember that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Page 2695 of our transcript, isn't it true that Mr. Murselovic "joked a little bit with the secretary, with Mica, and I told her: `Listen, Mica, the presidents here keep changing, but you are constant. You are also here.' She was the secretary for Mr. Cehajic before." And so -- another quote, Mr. Murselovic told you: "Well, listen, Mica, the presidents keep coming and going, but you are here always."

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember those times. I even told him that when we had this private conversation when he was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. It was an informal conversation in which I told him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you at that time discuss with Muharem Murselovic the fact that Dr. Stakic occupied Mr. Cehajic's office within days of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember at all that Muharem was there. Therefore, I don't remember the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it ever discussed at that point in time that Dr. Stakic had or would go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then we really can come back to Dr. Minka Cehajic. Once again that we have the necessary follow up, we discussed this already beforehand, she tried to contact Dr. Stakic by telephone. And is it correct that you told her that Dr. Stakic and Kovacevic could not be reached?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I don't remember that, and especially not about Dr. Kovacevic, who was not sitting together with me and whose calls I couldn't put through even if I wanted to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be correct that Minka Cehajic tried for several times to reach, in this case, Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. And I'm really sorry for Minka if that indeed was the case, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you then later - maybe not in the office but in town or elsewhere - have a discussion with Dr. Cehajic on Professor Cehajic's fate?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Cehajic and I met, I believe it was last year, in the street where the restaurant Expres is. There were two other persons with us, and the gentleman who was with us suggested that we should sit on the terrace in front of the Expres restaurant and have a cup of coffee. The conversation was friendly and informal. We were asking after each other's children and what each of us was doing at the time and how we were. Things like that. None of us mentioned the period in question, the period that you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me try the other way around. You were the receptionist, we understood, opposed to the ordinary work of a secretary. But from your own assessment, seeing the visitors coming in and out, from your point of view, who was the more important person; the president, the vice-president?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a hierarchy. The president was on the top of that hierarchy, and he was followed by the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about the hierarchy when we take into account also the name of Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the municipality, it is the president and then the vice-president and the Executive Board is a different body, and Dr. Kovacevic was its head. And then there were heads of various services or departments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From your point of view as a citizen of Prijedor, who was, in terms of influence, political influence, the high-ranking person; Dr. Stakic as the president of the Municipal Assembly, or Kovacevic in his area?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as politics go, I don't know. But if we're talking about administrative body, the influence on the assembly, on the administrative bodies, Stakic was the president of the assembly, and Dr. Kovacevic was the president of the Executive Board, which indicates that Dr. Kovacevic had influence on administrative organs because they were under the authority of Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So once again, the question I have put to you already: Did you see Dr. Kovacevic in Dr. Stakic's office?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This happen --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But not in the office. They would pass by me, so I would see them passing by. And when he entered or when I entered, then obviously, he would ask me what I was going to drink, for example. But that was only when I was invited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How often did this happen that both of them came together? To the best of your recollection, of course.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To go through my office, I don't remember the number of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Frequently, daily, weekly, monthly?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not need to see each other every day. Maybe once or twice a week, or even less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take it from your testimony that you were invited going for a drink together with them. Is this correct, or was this a misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a misunderstanding. That was a misunderstanding. They would invite me, they would call me and ask me to order a drink for them. We had a kitchen, a kitchenette, and a person working there. So I would call that person and I would order drinks for Dr. Stakic or for Dr. Kovacevic if he was in Dr. Stakic's office. I would ask them to bring a cup of coffee or something, whatever they asked me to order for them. I never had a drink with any president ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. And I take it from this that apparently you told us yesterday the limited responsibility you had at that time, and you were not at all involved, for example, preparing a cup of coffee for Dr. Stakic or any visitor. You would ask others to bring this to the office. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that we spoke about coffee yesterday. But you are right. If somebody wanted coffee in their office, I would call this lady who worked in the kitchenette, and I would ask her to bring the coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm following the order of the transcript, and therefore it leads me to page 80, yesterday it was discussed what happened in July 1997. On line 12, you said: "I had been on sick leave for almost two months." When you came back to office, who was in both rooms you mentioned previously and indicated on Exhibit J26? This was your sketch. Were both offices occupied or only one?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both offices were empty, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I would ask, me myself, coming back from a sick leave for almost two months, the president not there, vice-president not there, what did you do? Whom did you ask what to do?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not return after two days after the day in question but after more than a month, so that I don't know what I did, whether I asked somebody or not. I can't remember. I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When was it that the one -- that Dr. Stakic or both positions, that there was a replacement, if so?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date when that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is easy to understand due to the course of time. But who were the next ones in the line of your bosses? We learned that you had apparently up to 13 presidents, and maybe then later even a mayor. But who was the next in line following Dr. Stakic, and when did he arrive, or she maybe?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the year 1997, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Borislav Maric who came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: She was then acting as the president of the Municipal Assembly at that time, or already as mayor? I'm sorry, I'm not aware when this change happened.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Maric stayed in the position for quite some time, until the arrival of the lady who replaced him in the year 2000. And I don't know how long Borislav Maric stayed. Well, this is an example to show that I really don't know how long people stayed in office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following your long career, this is easy to understand, no doubt. Page 82 of yesterday's transcript, you mentioned that it was not for you to take care that Dr. Stakic received documents, newspapers, or the Official Gazette. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the takeover, we received Politika, Oslobodenje, and Glas regularly. When Kozarski Vjesnik started being printed, I don't know when that was, and I don't know who brought it to our office. But in any case, Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 11134 to 11144. we would find it on our desks in the morning when we arrived at work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this was -- it arrived daily, both the Kozarski Vjesnik, and then later, as we have seen it, the wartime edition of Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozarski Vjesnik is a weekly, and it was published on Fridays, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you received Kozarski Vjesnik, all of you, you as the person responsible for the reception of persons, the president and the vice-president. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive it. It was not envisaged for me to receive it. When I say press, I have in mind the period before the takeover and after the takeover. So the press arrived for both the president's office and the service, that is, the technical service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification, on page 48, line 25, you stated, "Up to the takeover, we received Politika, Oslobodenje, and Glas regularly. When Kozarski Vjesnik started being printed, I don't know when that was, and I don't know who brought it to our office. But in any case, we would find it on our desks in the morning when we arrived at work." So this was what confused me, reading the "we received it." What means "we"?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We. I may have used the wrong word. I would find a stack of four or five copies. I would give one to the president, the other to the vice-president, and the other copies would be sent throughout the different services. If I needed one, I had to put it away somehow because we weren't getting a sufficient number of copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the final question before the break: What about the Official Gazette? Was it the same approach taken there, that it also arrived with you and then distributed?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Official Gazette, I'm not sure when it was printed. Someone from the services - because that's where it was printed - would bring it to the president, so there was no need for me to know what the agenda of the assembly would be. Those were just brief overviews of the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the agenda of the assembly. I only asked whether or not in -- put it more generally: In the office of the president, in your office, or in the office of the vice-president, there was this Official Gazette available.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Official Gazette, as I've said, would be brought by someone from the services when, I suppose, one of the secretaries -- employees, I don't think they only came for the Official Gazette. Maybe there were other things or documents. And then they would give the Official Gazette to both the president and the vice-president. When the Official Gazette was published and when they began publishing, when they first began publishing, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance until now. We'll have a break now. And therefore, the trials stays adjourned until half past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.05 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May the witness please be shown Document S180. Immediately before the break, we discussed questions related to the Official Gazette. It's now more than ten years, but would you identify this document as Official Gazette 2 of 1992, dated the 25th June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Official Gazette had exactly this kind of heading. That should be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and have a look on item number 117.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't seem to find it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was just a random decision to ask you to have a look on 117. If you could have a look, for example, on 115, did you ever see these kinds of decisions, conclusions, orders or whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision specifically, I have never seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In general, did you see decisions taken by the Crisis Staff and then appearing in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't need to read the Official Gazette, and I happen to know what it looks like from the time I worked in the technical services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the question, you can see here on this example, this document, a typewritten, signed by Dr. Milan Kovacevic. The one before was signed by Dr. Stakic. Do you know what was the reason that some decisions were signed by Dr. Kovacevic, some by Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic at any point in time approach you, telling you that it's impossible that these decisions bearing his name -- if you, on perusal, you will see that most of the decisions were signed by Dr. Stakic in this Official Gazette 2 of 1992, that they were signed allegedly by him. Did he ever tell you this was not correct, there was something wrong with these signatures?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never said anything like that, nor did we ever discuss anything along these lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then ask the witness be shown Exhibit Number S79. In the moment, we are not interested in the contents of this document, but if you could be so kind and look on the signature. And do we have the B/C/S original version? Okay, thank you. If, please, the B/C/S version could be put on the ELMO. What would be your comment, without any questions, related to this signature block on the right-hand side of the bottom lines of the document?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Dr. Stakic's signature. If you had hidden the part towards the top, if you only made me read what's written towards the bottom of the page, I wouldn't even be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the stamp we can see here? Where in your office or Dr. Stakic's office was actually the stamp?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
