utterances.text: That was in the technical services; neither of the offices you have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it was your testimony that neither stamped -- any of the documents were stamped in the office of Dr. Stakic or in your office. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't in my office. And in Dr. Stakic's office, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Tell me, from my experience in former communist countries, were your offices locked in the evening by seal?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Never. I would come to work, and the office would be unlocked. There was even a fire usually left burning during the time there was no heating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there a special cupboard for different stamps to be used in office?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any stamps. I didn't see any stamps being used. I guess that's self-implicit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "We" means you and Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and the vice-president, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the whole of the president's office, as you previously testified on page 52, line 21, that was in the technical services. And you are quite sure that the stamps were attached at the technical services unit?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that, I meant the usual work performed by the technical services, the technical services unit. If you show me one from the Crisis Staff, I really don't know who did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You're talking now about a stamp used by the Crisis Staff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it looks like. I don't even know who put the stamps there for the Crisis Staff, on behalf of the Crisis Staff. I really don't know. Wherever I say, I would only be guessing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Then please leave the document with the witness, and show the witness now Exhibit Number S71. As usual, the best possible, and if possible, even the colour copy. Would you please comment once again on the signature and stamp block, and compare the two documents you have before you.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the signature. I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is there a difference between the two signatures?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By just looking at it, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So why this? You're more acquainted with your mother language than we are. Can you see the reason why we have two different signatures, apparently?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shape is different. Can't read either of these signatures. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then leave also the two documents with the witness, and show -- the witness may be shown Exhibit 79. Once again, the signature block, can you identify "Za" in front of the typed name Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see some of the stamp, but I can't see "Za" written anywhere. Perhaps it is, but I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would it mean if there would be a "Za" in front of the signature?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my own experience, that means that someone else is signing on behalf of the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On which occasion was it necessary that somebody else signed on behalf of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't even assume. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's take the scenario, a person, as you told us, is coming in. He or she wants to have the signature of Dr. Stakic. He's not available. To whom would you send this person interested to have the signature as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whoever brought something to be signed, that person should know who's in charge of signing the paper. It wasn't up to me to decide such issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So your testimony is you are not aware who was in charge in case Dr. Stakic was not available to sign documents if necessary. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't know. I'm not a lawyer, to know about what other people's authorities were. That's a purely legal matter, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe one can have a different view and see it as a more practical matters that one knows who has to sign, and therefore sent the requesting person immediately to the person in charge. But your testimony is quite clear, and so therefore, we have to take it as it is. But let's have two additional documents. Leave the others, please, with the witness. And then Exhibit S70, 7-0. What about signature, what about stamp?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that the stamp is of the Municipal Assembly. And the signature, I'm really not familiar with this signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then if you have a look to the left-hand side, in front of the date 9 June 1992, what can we read there?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the date? The date beneath the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. The word in front of the 9. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. This is illegible. I can't read this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then please go to the top of this page, right-hand side. Yes, thank you. What can we read there?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says "Jankovic," and "Prpos".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was Mr. or Mrs. Jankovic or Prpos, do you know?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would be a difficult assumption to make just by looking at this family name. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. What about the filing system? Let us take -- stay for a moment with this document. When such a document was filed, do you have a central registry or registrar where all these documents were archived, or was it the case that in order that the one signing documents had an overview of what he had signed in the past, that one copy was left in the office of the signing person?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a special filing room in which all the documents that reach the Municipal Assembly end up. And then documents are forwarded through the records to a certain service or department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's your testimony none of the copies would be left by the signator in his or her office?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know. You asked me about the general method of keeping records, incoming records. I don't think that even existed in terms of all documents that were signed being recorded in some sort of a filing archive. I don't think there was such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And then may the witness please be shown additionally Document S96. And once again, please, concentrate on this block, the signature and stamp block. What can you read there?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with this signature. It's typed very clearly, so I may be able to assume what's written there, but the signature itself, I don't recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In this case, I don't want only -- not only to refer to the signature, but also to the words typed. Would you please read them aloud.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "President of the Assembly of the Serbian people of Prijedor Municipality." I didn't realise that that was the official name. Serbian people. God forbid. I really don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then the name typed there?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see typed here is Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And can you identify the stamps? And especially the left-hand stamp, the insignia in this stamp?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the coat of arms bears the letters SDS. But I don't recognise the entire stamp. I do know some of these marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And then additionally, S101. What can you identify there, be it handwritten or be it typed, the signature block?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recognise anything. The only thing I can do is read it out. But it doesn't remind of anything I had seen before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. In this case, we have to add another exhibit, 172, please. Can you identify this document?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I see for the first time that there was some record of people who attended a session. This is absolutely unknown to me, something like that. I'm absolutely not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then thank you for this at the moment. And the documents may be returned to Madam Registrar. Totally different topic: We touched briefly upon it yesterday. At what point in time did Dr. Stakic wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was only on some very few occasions, when he would go to see the recruits off. I really didn't make a note of these things. They were not relevant, and it is really very unusual for me to have to think back on those occasions after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were you yourself ever asked to wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I wore civilian clothes, and I just did my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there ever a duty for members of part of the civil servants, be it the Executive Board or others, to wear uniforms at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the military wore uniforms. We were an administrative body, and just civil servants, just -- and the employees of that body never wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore, my question: Did you see Dr. Stakic in his office wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he would come to the office, and then he would go to see the recruits off. And he only wore uniform on those occasions. I'm not talking about people being sent to war, but young people, young men who were recruits and who were being sent to the regular army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Milovan Dragic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know Dragic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Milovan Dragic.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Dragic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: He was a visitor to Dr. Stakic's office?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- for being not concrete. When I ask you this line of questions, it's always related to the period of time after the takeover until the end of 1992. So to the best of your recollection, you don't know. If so --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Transcript page 10.526, Mr. Dragic testified, on line 25: "Members of the Executive Board wore uniforms, too, but only for a very brief while." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't even know who the members of the Executive Board were. I'm sorry. If you refer to the members of the Executive Board, I really don't know. And that is what I'm reading in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But what about the persons living together or working together with you on the same corridor on the first floor of the municipal building? For example, Mr. Kovacevic and his deputy, did they wear, at a certain point in time, uniforms in office?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that as being an obligation. I remember Dr. Kovacevic wearing running shoes, Adidas shoes, and a pair of worn-out blue jeans. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But please, this was not the question. The question was: Did you see Mr. Kovacevic in office wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't go to his office, and I don't remember that he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Without quoting a name, because it was in closed session, page 7563, when Dr. Stakic wore a camouflage uniform, did he, in addition, wear a belt around his waist and had a pistol tucked away in his belt?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Experience shows that extraordinary incidents or accidents are recalled easily. So wouldn't it be extraordinary if you would see your boss wearing a pistol tucked away in his belt?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I should be able to remember that, but I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic wear a camouflage uniform the day after the attack? I make reference to transcript pages 3209, following.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May then I ask the video unit to play the first video. This is - please assist me - exhibit number S7. Could it please be started. Today I can't see anybody through the glass. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So stop, please. May I ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I first ask the video unit to try to fix that we have a kind of a still -- yes, thank you. Can you identify persons sitting here?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljaja, and the others I can't recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where would Zeljaja sit? We have five persons.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the left-hand side or to the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can read that it's 11:36:34:03, and this would be the person immediately over 34:03. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could please rewind the video. Very short. Stop. Can you now identify additional persons?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see Budimir and Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Budimir would be seated where, please?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my right. Looking from my position, he is on the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Beside Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript, it's now 11:36:30:13. And could you please rewind a little bit further. Okay. This was not helpful. Please play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. On the left-hand side, you can identify a person?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then please continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. Do you know one of these three persons? We are now at 11:36:37:02.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please continue playing the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. We are now at 11:36:46:21.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very dark, so I can't see very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it better now for you?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't see their faces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please continue with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Whenever you see a person you know, please stop. You didn't see anybody else whom you would know?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please, wind it forward once again. Say stop, please, when you --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, stop. I can see Dragan Savanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 11:37:06:02. This would be the person seated in the middle of the three persons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Anybody else you identified during --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's conclude with this video, and then go immediately to the next video. This would be S157. Correct? Please start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can see the persons sitting here?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can see Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you see Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you see him wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't see it in this photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then, please, rewind the video. Please rewind the video to the beginning. Stop. Just the first seconds of the video. Stop.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And was this one of the occasions you previously told us Dr. Stakic would wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this occasion is. I don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please play the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can identify the lady sitting there?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you maybe rewind a little or forward it a little, if possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's, please, rewind a little bit, and then forward, and then --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe zoom it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's stop here. Try whether you can see it. Can you identify the lady?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see very well. I'm not sure that I do. I think it may be Mrs. Balaban, but I'm not sure because I don't see it very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At what occasion were you asked to call Madam Balaban?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that foreign journalists were there at the time, or something like that. I don't know what kind of a meeting that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And can you try to explain to us why the persons we are -- we can see on this still and on other occasions, being members of the Executive Board or of the police or the army or of the Municipal Assembly, as we can see in front of us, Dr. Stakic wearing uniforms, not only for this official ceremonies, as you told us previously, but when international journalists arrived. Why is this?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please, Your Honour -- I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us previously that on special occasions, special ceremonies, it was the custom of that Dr. Stakic at least wore a uniform. Now we can see here on the video that not only Dr. Stakic, but also other representatives, be it from the Executive Board, be it from the police, be it from the military, wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to now tell you why they wore uniforms on that occasion? I really don't understand what is expected of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you give us the reason why, based on this video, based on the testimony of other witnesses, having seen Dr. Stakic, Dr. Kovacevic wearing uniforms in the building where you worked, in uniform? What was the reason why a president of a Municipal Assembly wore a uniform, why a president of the Executive Board wore a uniform?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I can't see that this is really a uniform on the president of the Executive Board. I don't know what kind of a meeting this is. Was that maybe on that day when he was supposed to see the recruits off, and then after that he attended this meeting? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now turn to some remaining topics. Thank you, in the direction of the video unit. We can stop this now. During yesterday's testimony, LiveNote page 84, line 19 through 21, you were asked: "Decisions within the competence of the Municipal Assembly. In other words, the work that the Municipal Assembly would normally do, the decisions that they would normally make, who was making those decisions when the Municipal Assembly was not meeting in 1992?" Answer: "I don't know. The assembly wasn't meeting. There were no written decisions to be made, so I don't know." How did you know that the assembly wasn't meeting, having learned that you didn't have any calendar, any kind of schedule, any kind of overview of the work exercised by Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply couldn't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you explicitly stated, "The assembly wasn't meeting." What brings you to this testimony?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the last meeting of the assembly was held when Bosnia and Herzegovina seceded from Yugoslavia. I don't know when they met again after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For a better understanding, you just said: "I think the last meeting of the assembly was held when Bosnia and Herzegovina seceded from Yugoslavia." What has this to do with the internal affairs in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that that was when the last meeting of the assembly took place. And after that, I don't really know whether there were any further meetings or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The second part of your answer yesterday was: "There were no written decisions to be made, so I don't know." What brings you to your testimony? What's the underlying basis for this testimony that you can state that there were no written decisions to be made?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question, Your Honour. Because I'm not sure what I meant yesterday when I said that. So if I can just have the question repeated, I'll try to think back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I want to repeat your answer in context. When asked whether or not there was a Municipal Assembly meeting in 1992, your answer was: "I don't know. The assembly wasn't meeting. There were no written decisions to be made, so I don't know." My question was: What brings you to the testimony that there were no written decisions to be made, having stated previously that you were not involved at all in the preparation and execution of written decisions?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could have heard when the meeting of the assembly was supposed to be held. Some of the people I worked with would probably have brought up the subject. They would say something like, "We're going to the meeting." So that's the only way I could have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But my question was related to exactly why did you know that there were no written decisions to be made?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any. They didn't pass through my hands, not before that point and not after that point. So I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But read in context, you stated: "The assembly wasn't meeting. There were no written decisions to be made." Normally, one could conclude from this that, previously, written decisions were made when the assembly was meeting, but not later on. Is this assessment wrong?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I can say is, again, when there was a meeting of the assembly, I wouldn't know the date because the whole of the department would go, or many people from the department would go to attend the meeting. And usually, they would tell me that they would be absent. Whenever the president went to an assembly meeting, or the vice-president, and when I said what I said yesterday, what I must have meant was that throughout that period, there were no such moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be now your testimony that when the assembly met, you were informed by Dr. Stakic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have known that he was going to an assembly meeting. Some people from the department would tell me, or Dr. Stakic could have said it himself, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And apropos meeting, when we saw the video just some minutes before, did you identify the room where this meeting with the journalists was held? Was this a conference room? Was it a room where the assembly was meeting? Unfortunately, we all don't know, so if you could be kind enough and assist us in identifying the room we saw.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the hall where the assembly was meeting, because that hall must be much bigger in order to be able to seat all the deputies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in which room met the Crisis Staff; in the one we saw on the video or in the room where normally the assembly met?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't recognise this particular room, nor do I know where Crisis Staff meetings were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Page 85 of yesterday's testimony, when asked about documents, you stated on line 8: "No, I never brought him any documents to be signed." And then you added: "Not even before the war." What does it mean, "never brought him any documents to be signed, not even before the war"? Why this distinction between the time before and after the war?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I really wanted to say is that it wasn't part of my job. It wasn't part of my job before the war, it wasn't part of my job during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think on page 94, 95 of yesterday's testimony, you told us that in July 1992, Dr. Stakic received Mr. Zupljanin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was a slip of the tongue. Zupljanin used to come -- because the Prosecutor had mentioned -- I can't remember what his name was. And then I said no, because there were two persons being referred to by the Prosecutor. Zupljanin used to come before the war, yes. Before the takeover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And he met with whom? Was he alone with Dr. Stakic or were other persons present at a meeting with Mr. Zupljanin? Sorry that I can't pronounce correctly the name.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're doing fine. Zupljanin came in April, immediately after the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was supposed to meet with Dr. Cehajic in the small hall. I remember that day. I opened the door of the small hall, small meeting room, and Mr. Mirza - I think his last name was Mujadzic - and Zupljanin came in. When I called the lady who worked in the restaurant, in the canteen, after some ten minutes, I thought it was time for the others to come in, too. The lady from the cafeteria went to the meeting room, and then she came back to me, saying there's no one there in the room. I went into Dr. Cehajic's office. He was sitting at his table, reading papers. He said: "There's no meeting." He gave no explanation. So this meeting seems to have ended before it even began. And that's why I remember the moment and the day of Zupljanin's visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to be absolutely --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to be absolutely on the safe side, it is your testimony that there was no meeting with Mr. Zupljanin in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is my submission that there was no meeting with Mr. Zupljanin. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And then on transcript page 102, line 3, you mentioned that Dr. Stakic had a driver. Did he have only one driver or several drivers?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please, for a short moment, in closed session -- or private session is enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's absolutely correct that you asked me to rephrase the question. I should have asked you first, was there a departure and voluntary exodus from Prijedor Municipality prior to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were leaving, people of non-Serbian ethnicity, in great numbers. You could notice it about the town outside the hotel. The Balkan Hotel, I would often pass it on my way to the supermarket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the reason that, as you said, people of non-Serbian ethnicity were leaving the town prior to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned, just by chance, the Balkan Hotel. Did you ever make an appointment or put through a telephone call from or to Dr. Stakic in September 1992 to a hotel in preparation of a meeting of representatives from the entire region?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We previously touched upon this issue already, but could you please tell us why it was that at the same time a number of persons resigned or were compelled to resign or even dismissed together with Dr. Stakic in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You worked together with the person who replaced Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for the purpose of transcript, the name of this person replacing Dr. Stakic, once again, was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Dusan Kurnoga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss with Mr. Dusan Kurnoga the reasons why Dr. Stakic was replaced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's go for a moment in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I requested private session. Thank you for assisting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Madam Radakovic, can you tell us who telephoned Dr. Stakic regularly or more often than others between April 1992 and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. At least not in those terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did representatives of Bosnian Serb political and military leadership ever contact Dr. Stakic? I mean Mr. Radovan Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, General Ratko Mladic, and the like?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I have never seen any of them. I have never seen any of these people you've just referred to in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Whom Dr. Stakic telephoned very often, on a regular basis, let us say?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any particular obligations to make any regular calls, nor do I remember any such regular calls to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Next question: Who visited the office of Dr. Stakic on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a regular basis, I don't know. People would come, people from the body we worked in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: More or less often than others.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly people from administrative bodies, managers on different levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did Dusan Baltic ever visit the office of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretary of the assembly? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: How often? Once a week, twice a day --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only rarely. I can't remember the exact frequency. It's really difficult to say. We had clients coming in, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What about Spiro Marmat?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I know that he worked in the Secretariat for Defence. It was under the -- now it's the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And the last question: Was Dr. Stakic absent from his office from time to time due to the official business trips outside Prijedor or Prijedor Municipality during the period between April and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any such absences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 25 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And please, Judge Argibay, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, madam. I have a few questions to put to you. The first one relates to the April the 30th, remember, the day when you went to your work, found two young soldiers who looked at your identity card or something to that -- in that way, and let you in, and the day you said that Dr. Stakic came as usual to work. May I ask, did he look surprised at what was happening in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Dr. Stakic when I first entered the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I don't mean --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He looked normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: He looked normal. You saw him afterwards. He was there already when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but I am not sure. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. You were not surprised, you yourself, that Professor Cehajic didn't arrive to work?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised. Of course I was. After the telephone call and after my friend told me what she told me, my second surprise came when I entered the building. And a third surprise of that day was the fact that Cehajic didn't come to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And didn't it surprise you that Dr. Stakic was not surprised at the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't actually tell whether he was either surprised or not surprised. We didn't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I'm changing to another point, and I want to come back to your sketch of the municipal building and the quarrel or discussion you heard in Dr. Stakic's office between Dr. Stakic and Mr. Drljaca. You told us, and I saw in this sketch you made, that your window gives on to a balcony, and that you can go through the balcony to the other offices, the ones that are beside your office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe for a better --

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- it's appropriate to put J26 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Was the argument in very loud voices, as I understand, correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a discussion. There was noise, a quarrel, an argument, a loud argument. Something was happening during that discussion. Some different interests and views were expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You don't know what was the matter of that thing, the subject properly?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear anything, and I stood up to close the window, that is, the door, for the purpose of not being able to hear the discussion because I was not interested in hearing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I can understand that. Wouldn't it better to go out on the balcony and close the windows of Dr. Stakic's office from the outside?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not necessary because the only place where their conversation could be heard was in my office, close to my window. There is another window in the other office, and then after that there is a small conference room with nobody there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And you couldn't hear anything through the door, for instance?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Through the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's change the subject, please. You told us today in, I think it was, for the benefit of the parties, page 66, line 9, you told Judge Schomburg that the last meeting of the Municipal Assembly was held when Bosnia and Herzegovina seceded. Do you remember the date of the secession?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the 4th of April -- no, the 6th of April. I remember the date because on that same day, the 6th of April, during the Second World War, Belgrade was bombarded, was shelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And so it's your memory that after April the 6th, 1992, there were no more assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember that there were any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And are you aware that the political parties at that moment, being a part of the assembly having the deputies, the president who was Professor Cehajic, another who was the vice-president who was Dr. Stakic, and all the people involved in the Municipal Assembly were taking some measures, proposing something to go on?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any conclusions or decisions from the sessions of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Where in the building did the Municipal Assembly meet?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at that time, the sessions were held in an adjacent building, next to the building of the municipality. There was no room in the building of the municipality that would be suitable for the purpose. So in that period, I believe that they allocated the other building for a longer period of time, not only for that session, but for a longer period of time, it was that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And in reference to what you told us in page 71, line 21, about the lot of non-Serb persons leaving Prijedor before the 30th of April, 1992, you said that you did not know the cause for this exodus, as Judge Schomburg asked you. Did you ever ask someone, the families of these persons, why were so many people leaving Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You weren't interested in knowing why your neighbours were leaving?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I had known why they were leaving, I would have left myself. Maybe I would have been better off if I had left at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Can you explain this answer. I really don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If there was a good reason for them to leave, then I should have left myself. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have only one, Your Honour. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Radakovic, Judge Schomburg asked you today on page 45, line 12 and onwards, something about the hierarchy in the Municipal Assembly. I would like to ask you something about the secretary-general of the Municipal Assembly. Is the secretary-general of the Municipal Assembly an official of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the secretary-general responsible? Does he answer to the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the president of the Municipal Assembly the secretary-general's boss, superior? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The president of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I use the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't think we got the interpretation of the answer because counsel started his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I put a double negative question, so maybe Your Honour can ask. I don't want to be in jeopardy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to step into the shoes of the Defence. Therefore, please repeat the question and break it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the president of the Municipal Assembly boss of the secretary-general of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He is not his boss, but he is not my boss either. But he is an official who is appointed to serve the president and the vice-president. And my obligations are only towards the secretary-general, and he is the one who is in charge of signing the documents about my salary and other similar documents. And he does the same thing for the president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Two short areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, you talked about in 1997 when you came back from having your teeth fixed, and both the office of the president and vice-president were empty, the president having been Dr. Stakic. Is it correct that the vice-president in 1997, who also was not there following the arrest of Dr. Kovacevic, was Momcilo Radanovic, otherwise known as Cigo?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And Cigo left Prijedor at the same time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that when I came back to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. The other short area is on page 103 of yesterday's transcript, line 14, you were asked: "Did Dr. Stakic wear a gun?" And you answered: "Not that I saw." I would like to go back to the video that you were shown last, S157. I have asked for just one still to be shown from that video, if you could look at your monitor. Stop. Ma'am, do you see the gun on the right-hand hip of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: STOJA RADAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. It's very dark. Secondly, I don't know where this is, what was the occasion. Maybe this was not the building of the Municipal Assembly at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could just go a couple frames further. Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the registry and the audio unit -- the video unit, please prepare a still of this picture we just saw. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any further questions? I can't see any questions. Then, I have to thank you for accompanying us through this long journey through documents, videos, exhibits. I hope you have got the impression that we try to highlight that what happened in 1992 to your country, to your hometown, to yourself, and to your neighbours from all perspectives, not only from one side. And only this enables us to come to a final judgement on individual criminal responsibility, if so. And this is the task we have to exercise because we strongly believe that there must be justice, and there will be no peace without justice. And we can't obtain justice without coming as close as possible to the truth. And thank you for assisting us in this work, and I wish you a safe trip home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, it's always your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't need to be. I value this Tribunal greatly. I can see that you're working very hard, that you have a lot of work to do. We follow your work on television. I didn't know it would be so long and thorough. I'm sorry if I couldn't help you with some details. The only reason I couldn't was my mental absence at the moments when this was all happening because, for me, the war began in 1990 at the moment when my son went to serve his compulsory military service. I suffered from depression because already at the time unrest could be felt in Croatia. My son was not released from the army when he was supposed to be released, when he completed his compulsory military service. I went to see what was going on, so his military service was extended due to the conditions that prevailed in Karlovac at the time. The barracks were -- was encircled. I had some legal possibilities available to me. Firstly, I could show his student's booklet, showing that he was a regular student at the university in Bihac in that year. That was 1991. But I did not have any contacts with my son over the telephone, so I had to go there, to physically go there. The barracks was encircled. When I asked for my son's superior officer, he was not there. And I went back home without my son. And that is something, an event that was really hard to live with. It would have been hard even for some men. And my son only returned when all of the barracks, all the manpower, moved out from the barracks. After a very short period of time, some six months or so, all these things that you were asking me about started happening in Prijedor, and I was not able to remember some of those things that you asked me about. And the only reason why I couldn't remember them is the fact that all throughout that time, I was under the impression and I was concerned, and I worried how to save my child, how to help him. When I couldn't help him, I had to pack him to go to the front line. So I witnessed that. Besides that, I lived in my household together with my father and my mother. My father was on heavy medication. He was wounded in the Second World War. Since then, he didn't have one leg. He suffered from asthma. Those were his regular complaints. And on top of those, there were some other complaints he had. Every day, day in, day out, I had to struggle to get food, to get the medication that was necessary, and I had very little time to think about the things that were happening at the time. Maybe that is the reason why I wasn't aware of things. Maybe that is the reason why I couldn't provide you with the information that you asked me about. On my way here, I realised, and then I saw that a lot of effort is being invested about the arrival of witnesses. Our accommodation is very good. I am here with the best intention to help you, the Honourable Judges, but Dr. Stakic as well. And if I was not convinced, if I was not sure that Dr. Stakic just found himself at a wrong place at a wrong time, and that things may have just been misrepresented in his case, if I wasn't convinced that he is innocent, I wouldn't be here. I would really regret the time that I have spent here if the contrary to what I believe was proven correct. Thank you for listening to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to thank you for your additional and very personal remarks. And it will assist us in a better understanding of your entire testimony. Once again, thank you for coming and, hopefully, having a safe trip home. May I ask the usher, please, to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Down to earth, we have to discuss now some administrative matters. May I ask you, what about the witnesses of next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the next week, we were in danger not to have a single witness because the rumours were spreading down there that the witnesses of the Defence are ill treated in front of this Tribunal, and we have many problems with providing the Defence with the witnesses. So we still don't know whether we will have anybody for next week. And if we do, we'll be able only to bring three witnesses. It's Witness 021, 088, and 090.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the other envisaged --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the presiding judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the other envisaged witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For now, they refuse to testify in front of this Tribunal. Also, in connection with this, we have to have on the record that Your Honour read to this witness statements of other witnesses. And when we tried to do it during the Prosecution case, the Prosecution witnesses, you ruled that it's forbidden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before making these statements, could you please offer some evidence for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you read from Dr. Minka Cehajic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, it's quite clear: The question is whether it was ever forbidden to put questions based on concrete testimony to other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will provide you with that, Your Honour, gladly. Also, when you cross-examined the witnesses of the Prosecution, you yourself never read to the witnesses of the Prosecution from the statements of other witnesses. So we just want to have this on the transcript. And we will find in the previous transcripts places where you ruled and forbid both the Defence and the Prosecution to present the statements of another witness to the present witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I first ask the Prosecution for submissions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just draw the distinction between reading from an out-of-court statement and reading from testimony and giving a witness an opportunity to comment upon other testimony that might refresh recollection or in which the witness may deny the other testimony. That's different from an out-of-court statement. As for the schedule next week, we will cooperate in any way we can so the Defence can get their witnesses. If at some point witnesses refuse to voluntarily come, there, of course, is the power of the Tribunal to subpoena witnesses to come to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And when you already start discussing this point, can you please tell us in a very concrete way what are the names or the numbers of the witnesses you're referring to refusing to testify because of that what I think you called it wrong or ill treatment by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our investigator informed us only about the names of the people who may come, and he complained the whole last week that he has a lot of problems in regard of this issue. And that's why I reacted yesterday also improperly, because I was aware of this problem. And I was aware that we might not have any witnesses tomorrow -- actually, the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you give us the name or the number of only one witness that refused or tries to refuse to come to this Court based on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know it by heart, and I don't have it written here. I have only three names of the people who are coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Will it be possible to have additional witnesses that we can fill in the entire time provided for us during the next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will do our best. The problem with our witnesses is that they need visas. And although the Witness and Victims Unit is trying their best, they need at least five working days to provide the witness with the visa. We'll try to have at least another one or two witnesses for the next week, although we cannot promise to be successful because of these restrictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As to the fact that you yourself stated that you reacted yesterday improperly, I don't want to go into further more details, but please, I would ask both parties, in future, to refrain from discussing these issues in front of a witness. And it may be also the result of these false and misleading statements by the Defence that there is this wrong impression. And therefore, I think on the basis of that what you stated today, we need not go any more into details of this what you said wrongly yesterday. But please refrain from doing so in the future. Could you please assist us with the number of witnesses in the final list of Defence witnesses updated the 7th of January 2003. There is no such 88 and 09.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's the registry's mistake, Your Honour. I have updated the list, and these witnesses are added now. I will provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So what, then, about the proffer of the next witness? When -- will it be possible -- I know you are working extremely hard also during the weekend -- to have it at least in the morning of Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll try to provide you on Sunday. I don't know whether it would be possible for you to find it, but maybe we can e-mail it on Sunday. We will try to make it on Saturday or Sunday at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we will be prepared to hear Witness 21 on Monday afternoon. Anything else for the next week to be discussed? Because we calculated that there would be in the moment 34 witnesses remaining, and among those witnesses, three witnesses -- at least three witnesses that will take us more than one day. And in all likelihood, two experts. And we have already arrived at Day 106. That means there are only remaining 34 additional days, maximum. So it will be extremely difficult to follow our schedule in case there is no -- at one point in time, no witness available. And as I said since December, there is no leeway to have additional time for hearing the Defence case. So whenever it's possible and you hear from your investigators, I think also the OTP will be ready to hear additional witnesses. And I can only encourage you to do the very best that we have, per week, five witnesses, if not six, available.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would -- hopefully, we will be able to provide more witnesses for this trial, but we worked every day this week, and we finished only three witnesses. So also Your Honours and the Prosecution might consider to cut shorter your examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we'll all try to do our very best in reaching this goal. And no doubt it also depends on the provided scope of what will be covered by a witness on the basis of your proffer. We are grateful that the proffer is now -- the last proffers have been reliable ones. But tell us when you feel not necessary to cover the one or other area, as it was done in the past. Is there any progress - and this is a point of real concern - any progress with the translations of the exhibits? And if not, please tell us where is the bottleneck and what is the name of the responsible person that we may speed up and assist you in speeding up with the translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know where the bottleneck is. But our documents have been divided to three parts, and we just received the first one finished. So we'll provide Your Honours and the Prosecution with our exhibits at the beginning of the next week. We have this weekend to photocopy what we received, and the rest in B/C/S. And I think that the Prosecution has everything in B/C/S already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Correct? It's already with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We've received several binders in B/C/S. I take counsel's word that it's everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. When can we expect the first bundle of translations, of translated documents, which would normally be 65 ter documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we like to say, to be on the safe side, on Tuesday. I cannot promise Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As regards the witnesses, once again, as already stated by the Prosecution, if a person you need for your purposes, and refusing for what reason soever to appear, don't hesitate, as you did in the past, to ask for a subpoena for this witness. We will let you be informed on the ongoing attempts to have the two witnesses you requested as Chamber witnesses as soon as possible available. Any other submissions by the parties? Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing else, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this concludes the hearings of this week. And we will continue, as foreseen, on Monday afternoon, same courtroom, a quarter past 2.00. The trial stays adjourned.
